title: Identity Column
description: Learn how to use the IDENTITY property to create an auto-incrementing column in SQL Server.

data.text: SQL Server Identity Column

Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Identity Column**. Learn how to use the IDENTITY property to create an auto-incrementing column in SQL Server. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Identity Column and be confident in applying it to your projects.
IDENTITY Syntax

data.title: IDENTITY Syntax
data.content: Defines an identity column with optional seed and increment values.

data.text: The seed is the value of the first row. The increment is the value added to the previous row's identity. The default is (1,1), meaning the first row is 1, the second is 2, and so on.

data.title: Create Table with Identity Column
data.content: Creates a person table with an identity column.

data.title: Insert and Return Identity Value
data.content: Inserts a row and returns the generated identity value.

data.alt: SQL Server Identity Column example showing first row with person_id of 1

data.text: Reusing Identity Values
SQL Server does not reuse identity values. If an insert fails or is rolled back, the identity value is lost and will not be generated again, resulting in gaps.

data.title: Failed Transaction Leaves Gap
data.content: Demonstrates how a failed transaction creates a gap in identity values.

data.text: Resetting the Identity Counter
Use DBCC CHECKIDENT to reset the identity counter:

data.title: Reset Identity Counter
data.content: Resets the identity counter to 0 after deleting all rows.

data.text: Key Takeaways

data.title: IDENTITY Column Key Points
points: Use IDENTITY to create an auto-incrementing primary key column.
The default seed and increment are both 1.
SQL Server does not reuse identity values — gaps may occur.
Use DBCC CHECKIDENT to reset the identity counter.
Each table can have only one identity column.

data.text: Comprehensive Code Example

This example demonstrates a production-ready implementation of **Identity Column**. Study the code carefully, paying attention to error handling, type safety, and best practices. Try running it yourself and experiment with variations to deepen your understanding.

data.title: Production-Ready Implementation: Identity Column
data.content: Complete working example demonstrating best practices and common patterns.
data.code:
-- SQL Example with Best Practices
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spent,
    AVG(o.order_total) AS average_order
FROM 
    sales.customers c
LEFT JOIN 
    sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND o.order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, GETDATE())
WHERE 
    c.is_active = 1
    AND c.created_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY 
    c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING 
    COUNT(o.order_id) > 0
ORDER BY 
    total_spent DESC
OPTION 
    (RECOMPILE);

-- Performance Tips:
-- 1. Use appropriate indexes on join columns
-- 2. Avoid SELECT * - specify only needed columns
-- 3. Filter early with WHERE clause
-- 4. Use JOINs instead of subqueries when possible

data.text: Performance Considerations

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Identity Column**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.

**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
